name: self-serving-bias
description: A cognitive or perceptual process that is distorted by the need to maintain and enhance one's self esteem.
example:
Positive: A manager says her team's successful quarter reflects her leadership, but the failed quarter was due to market conditions beyond her control. Why: Success is attributed internally and failure externally by the same subject, protecting self-image.
Negative: A student says he passed because he studied hard and failed another exam because he didn't study enough. Why: Both outcomes receive internal attributions, so there is no self-protective asymmetry.
procedure: Locate each statement in the passage where a person or group explains the cause of an outcome involving themselves.
Classify each outcome as favorable (success, praise, gain) or unfavorable (failure, blame, loss) for the speaker.
For each attribution, note whether the cause cited is internal (ability, effort, character) or external (luck, others, environment, conditions).
Flag the pattern only when favorable outcomes are paired with internal causes AND unfavorable outcomes are paired with external causes by the same subject.
Verify the pattern serves self-esteem protection or enhancement, rather than being justified by evidence presented in the passage.
Confirm at least one success-internal and one failure-external pairing coexist before marking the pattern as present.
when_to_use: When asked to detect asymmetric causal attribution in which a speaker credits themselves for positive outcomes while blaming external factors for negative ones.
constraints: Do not flag cases where only successes or only failures are discussed; both polarities must appear.
Do not flag attributions that the passage independently supports with evidence, even if they favor the speaker.
Do not flag third-party attributions; the speaker and the subject of the outcome must be the same.
A single self-congratulatory or blame-shifting statement alone is insufficient without the contrasting pair.

name: accident-fallacy
description: an informal fallacy and a deductively valid but unsound argument occurring in a statistical syllogism (an argument based on a generalization) when an exception to a rule of thumb is ignored.
example:
Positive: An argument claims 'Taking others' property is theft; tax collectors take others' property; therefore tax collectors are thieves.' Why: It applies a rule-of-thumb to a case while ignoring the legal-authorization exception.
Negative: An argument claims 'All triangles have three sides; this figure is a triangle; therefore it has three sides.' Why: The major premise is universally true with no exceptions, so no exception is being overlooked.
procedure: Locate the general rule or generalization stated in the passage (often a broad claim like 'X is always Y' or 'all X are Y').
Identify the specific case or instance the argument applies the rule to.
Check whether the specific case has features that plausibly qualify as a recognized exception to the general rule (context, role, intent, legal permission, etc.).
Determine whether the argument ignores or suppresses that exception when drawing its conclusion about the specific case.
Confirm the argument's form is a statistical or rule-of-thumb syllogism rather than a universally true premise, and flag it only if an overlooked exception is what drives the faulty conclusion.
when_to_use: when asked to detect or diagnose an argument that applies a general rule to a specific case while overlooking a legitimate exception to that rule.
constraints: Do not flag arguments whose major premise is genuinely exceptionless rather than a generalization.
Do not flag arguments where the specific case does not actually fall under a recognized exception.
Require that both a generalization and an ignored qualifying exception be identifiable; missing either element disqualifies the match.
Do not confuse this with hasty generalization, which moves from cases to a rule rather than from a rule to a case.

name: complex-question-loaded-question-with-implicit-assumption
description: A question that is loaded with an implicit assumption.
example:
Positive: A question asks 'When did you stop cheating on the exams?' in a context where cheating has not been established. Why: Any dated answer concedes prior cheating, which was never agreed to.
Negative: A question asks 'Why did the suspect confess?' in a passage that has already stated the suspect confessed. Why: The presupposition is an established fact in the passage, not a smuggled assumption.
procedure: Locate every interrogative sentence in the passage or challenge.
For each question, list the propositions that must already be true for the question to make sense (its presuppositions).
Test each presupposition by asking whether a direct answer ('yes' or explanation) would force the respondent to concede that proposition.
Check whether the presupposition is contested, unestablished, or unfavorable to the respondent rather than mutually accepted background.
Mark the question as carrying an implicit assumption only if at least one presupposition is both non-trivial and not conceded elsewhere in the passage.
Record which specific proposition is being smuggled in, distinct from the surface question being asked.
when_to_use: Apply when asked to identify, analyze, or flag questions whose phrasing forces the answerer to accept an unstated or disputed claim.
constraints: Do not flag a question merely because it is pointed, accusatory, or emotionally charged if its presuppositions are already established facts.
Do not flag open-ended questions (who/what/why) that have no hidden claim beyond the topic itself.
Require that a direct answer logically entails agreement with the contested proposition; mere topical relevance is not enough.
Do not conflate a factual error inside a question with an embedded presupposition smuggled past the answerer.

name: red-herring
description: Introducing irrelevant points to detract attention from a question.
example:
Positive: A reporter asks a CEO why quarterly profits dropped, and the CEO replies that the company is deeply committed to innovation and employee wellbeing. Why: the reply swaps the specific profit question for unrelated positive themes without addressing it.
Negative: A reporter asks a CEO why quarterly profits dropped, and the CEO explains supply-chain delays before adding that the company remains committed to innovation. Why: the core question is directly answered, with the positive remark as supplement rather than substitution.
procedure: Locate the explicit question or challenge posed in the passage and write down its core subject.
For each response sentence, identify its actual topic and compare it to the question's subject.
Mark any response segment that shifts to a broadly appealing or tangential topic without answering the core subject.
Check whether the shift uses positive or emotionally resonant language to make the diversion seem like a natural reply.
Confirm that the original question remains unaddressed after the diversion before concluding the pattern applies.
when_to_use: when asked to detect a diversion in which a responder substitutes an irrelevant but appealing topic for a direct answer to a posed question.
constraints: Do not flag a response that genuinely addresses the question even if it includes additional praise or context.
Require both a clear question and a clear topic shift; a vague or partial answer alone is not sufficient.
Do not flag off-topic remarks that occur without any prior question prompting them.
Do not rely on tone alone; the response must fail to engage the question's actual subject.

name: metaphor
description: a figure of speech that, for rhetorical effect, directly refers to one thing by mentioning another.
example:
Positive: A passage states 'Her voice was a warm blanket on a cold night' when discussing how a speaker comforted listeners. Why: A voice (auditory) is directly equated with a blanket (tactile object) to transfer the quality of comfort without 'like' or 'as'.
Negative: A passage states 'Her voice was like a warm blanket on a cold night.' Why: The explicit comparison marker 'like' makes this a simile rather than a direct substitution of one thing for another.
procedure: Scan the passage for sentences that equate or substitute one noun/concept for another unlike thing.
For each candidate, confirm the comparison is direct (uses 'is', 'are', 'becomes', or renaming) rather than hedged with 'like' or 'as'.
Check that the two things compared belong to different categories or domains, so the statement is not literally true.
Infer the shared attribute the author wants transferred from the vehicle to the tenor (role, quality, function).
Match that inference to the challenge's question (identify, interpret, or apply) and select or construct the response accordingly.
Reject candidates whose comparison is literal, idiomatic-but-dead, or uses explicit comparison markers.
when_to_use: When asked to identify, interpret, or construct an implicit comparison where one thing is described as being another unlike thing without 'like' or 'as'.
constraints: Do not flag comparisons that use explicit markers such as 'like', 'as', 'resembles', or 'similar to'.
Do not flag statements that are literally true even if vivid; the two terms must belong to distinct categories.
Require a non-literal equation of two entities; mere descriptive adjectives or personification alone do not qualify.
Do not treat fixed idioms whose figurative sense has faded as instances of this device.

name: spatial-reasoning
description: The capacity to reason about the spatial relationships between objects.
example:
Positive: A passage says a ladder reached the second-story window, and the question asks what can be inferred about the ladder's length. Why: the reaching relation constrains a physical dimension derivable from the stated arrangement.
Negative: A passage says 'the argument fit the occasion' and the question asks about the argument's suitability. Why: 'fit' is used metaphorically, so no physical spatial inference is warranted.
procedure: Scan the passage for nouns referring to physical objects, containers, paths, or locations and list them.
For each pair of objects mentioned together, identify the spatial relation described (inside, above, beside, passing through, fitting into, blocking, etc.).
Translate each relation into an implied constraint on size, shape, position, or orientation (e.g., 'X fit into Y' implies X's relevant dimension ≤ Y's opening).
Check the challenge question against these derived constraints to see whether answering it requires inferring a spatial property not stated explicitly.
Combine multiple spatial constraints when needed to resolve the question, and verify the inference is consistent with every relation stated in the passage.
when_to_use: Use when the challenge requires inferring a physical property, position, or arrangement of objects from relational cues in the passage rather than from direct statements.
constraints: Do not apply when the passage's relations are purely metaphorical or social rather than physical.
Require that the inference follow from a stated spatial relation, not from world knowledge about the objects alone.
Do not over-specify dimensions the passage leaves underdetermined; infer only the relation the text supports.
One spatial word is not enough; confirm the relation actually constrains the property the question asks about.

name: modus-ponens
description: A syllogism that is of the form 'If P then Q. P. Hence Q.'
example:
Positive: A passage states 'If it rains, the match is canceled' and separately asserts 'It is raining,' prompting the student to infer the match is canceled. Why: the conditional and its affirmed antecedent are both present, yielding a valid consequent.
Negative: A passage states 'If it rains, the match is canceled' and separately asserts 'The match was canceled,' prompting an inference that it rained. Why: only the consequent is affirmed, which does not license concluding the antecedent.
procedure: Scan the passage for a conditional statement of the form 'if X then Y' (or equivalent phrasings like 'whenever X, Y' or 'X implies Y').
Identify the antecedent (the 'if' part) and the consequent (the 'then' part) of that conditional.
Search the passage for a separate assertion that the antecedent is true or has occurred.
Confirm the asserted fact matches the antecedent exactly, not a related or weaker claim.
If both the conditional and its affirmed antecedent are present, derive or select the consequent as the valid conclusion.
Reject the inference if the passage affirms the consequent, denies the antecedent, or introduces a different conditional structure.
when_to_use: when asked to evaluate whether a conclusion validly follows from a conditional premise paired with an affirmed antecedent.
constraints: Do not apply this pattern if only the consequent is asserted as true; that is a different and invalid inference.
Require both a conditional statement and an explicit affirmation of its antecedent before concluding.
Do not treat probabilistic or causal-sounding sentences as conditionals unless they establish a strict 'if-then' relationship.
Do not substitute a paraphrased or broader claim for the antecedent; the match must be exact in meaning.

name: statistical-syllogism
description: A syllogism that argues, using inductive reasoning, from a generalization true for the most part to a particular case.
example:
Positive: 'Most commuters in this city own a transit pass. Lena is a commuter here, so she likely has a transit pass.' Why: a majority premise plus individual membership yields a probabilistic conclusion about that individual.
Negative: 'All mammals have lungs. A whale is a mammal, so a whale has lungs.' Why: the major premise is universal, making this a deductive categorical syllogism rather than an inductive inference from a statistical majority.
procedure: Scan the passage for a generalization that holds for most (but not all) members of a group, using quantifiers like 'almost all', 'the majority', 'usually', or 'most'.
Locate a statement asserting that a specific individual or instance is a member of that group.
Check whether a conclusion is drawn (or is being asked) that applies the general trait to that specific member.
Verify the inference is inductive (probabilistic) rather than deductive: the premise must allow exceptions, not claim universality.
Confirm the three pieces align: the group in the generalization, the group in the membership claim, and the trait attributed to the individual must all match.
Flag or apply the pattern only when all three components (majority premise, membership premise, individual conclusion) are present and connected.
when_to_use: Use when asked to detect, classify, or evaluate an argument that moves from a 'most members have property P' premise plus an individual's group membership to a conclusion about that individual.
constraints: Do not flag arguments whose major premise is universal ('all' or 'none') rather than statistical.
Do not flag a standalone generalization that lacks an individual-case conclusion.
Require the group referenced in the generalization to be the same group the individual is said to belong to.
Do not treat a conclusion stated with certainty as equivalent when the premise is only probabilistic; note the inductive gap.

name: emotional-self-regulation
description: a complex process that involves initiating, inhibiting, or modulating one's state or behavior in a given situation.
example:
Positive: A character feels a surge of anger during an argument, takes a deep breath, and counts to ten before responding. Why: there is a clear trigger and a deliberate self-directed action to modulate the reaction.
Negative: A character speaks calmly throughout a pleasant conversation with a friend. Why: no emotional trigger is present and no modulation is occurring, so surface calmness does not qualify.
procedure: Locate the character or agent in the passage experiencing an emotional trigger or internal state shift.
Scan for explicit actions taken by that agent to initiate, inhibit, or modulate that state (pausing, breathing, reframing, delaying response, seeking calm).
Verify the action is self-directed and aimed at managing one's own emotion or behavior, not at changing the situation or another person.
Check that the modulation occurs in response to a specific emotional stimulus present in the passage.
Match the identified behavior against the challenge's question or acceptance criteria before selecting or labeling it.
when_to_use: when asked to detect or identify instances where a character consciously manages their own emotional state or behavioral response to a triggering situation.
constraints: Do not flag routine calm behavior that is not preceded by an emotional trigger.
Do not flag actions aimed at regulating another person's emotions rather than one's own.
Require both a triggering state and a deliberate modulating action; one alone is not sufficient.
Do not flag mere suppression that is involuntary or externally coerced.

name: folk-physics-common-knowledge-physics
description: The untrained human perception of basic physical phenomena.
example:
Positive: The challenge asks what happens to an unsupported cup nudged off a counter. Why: Gravity-driven falling is a universally expected everyday outcome resolvable by untrained intuition.
Negative: The challenge asks the terminal velocity of a feather in a specified air density. Why: It demands quantitative physics beyond common perception, so naive intuition is insufficient.
procedure: Scan the passage and challenge for references to everyday physical events (falling, rolling, floating, breaking, pouring, collisions, temperature changes).
For each referenced event, predict the outcome a typical untrained observer would expect based on gravity, inertia, buoyancy, or contact forces.
Compare that intuitive prediction against what the passage states or asks; note any gaps the challenge expects you to fill with common-sense physical reasoning.
Apply the intuitive prediction only to resolve the specific question posed, avoiding elaboration into formal physics equations or edge cases.
Confirm the physical claim involved is one an average person would accept without instruments or calculation before relying on this reasoning.
when_to_use: when the challenge hinges on predicting or interpreting an everyday physical outcome that an average person would infer without formal training
constraints: Do not invoke this reasoning for scenarios requiring quantitative calculation, specialized equipment, or expert-level physics.
Do not apply it when the passage explicitly overrides normal physical intuition (e.g., zero-gravity, fictional physics).
Require that the predicted outcome be one virtually any adult would agree on; uncertain or contested outcomes do not qualify.
Do not extend intuitive reasoning to microscopic, relativistic, or quantum phenomena where naive expectations fail.
